utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-R77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we were to continue this afternoon with the cross-examination of Witness Agnes. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'd call Mirsad Sahanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sahanic, I understand, sir, that you were born in Zvornik, in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court when you were born?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of June, 1970.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Can you also tell us what your ethnic background would be, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before the war began in the former Yugoslavia, sir, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you stationed as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Immediately before the war, I was working in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. How long had you been employed as a policeman prior to the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: For about four months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were stationed in Bosanski Samac, did you meet a young woman by the name of Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you know her before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly for about two months before the war began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that the Court is clear about what we're talking about, when the war began, can you give us the date that you're referring to as to when the war began? What date was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I am thinking of the date when Bosanski Samac was attacked; that is, when the war began in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you happen to remember what date in April of 1992 that may have been?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I think it was the 16th or 17th of April. It was a Saturday morning or, rather, the night between the Friday and Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll return to that, but before we do, I'm going to ask -- there is a folded white piece of paper to the left of the desk in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you show the witness the name written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. From now on, when I refer to a person by the name of Mr. Agnes, that is the person to whom I am referring, the person written on the piece of paper. Do you understand that, sir? You're nodding your head, indicating yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hopefully, sir, in your replies to any of my questions, I would ask that you refer to the person by the name of Mr. Agnes and not by the name written on that piece of paper. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the war beginning on the 16th or the 17th of April, 1992, did you become familiar with a person to whom I will refer as Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you known Mr. Agnes prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, for about two and a half months. I'm not quite sure, but I think it was that long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps now, sir, in your own words, would you share with us your relationship with Mr. Agnes and with the woman I referred to as Jasna? Can you just tell us, in your own words, how well you knew those people and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, I met Mr. Agnes, as he had a room in the hotel in Bosanski Samac where I was staying while I was employed, and that is how we met. We were together several times. As for Jasna, I met her a little later in a cafe in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how you met Jasna in a cafe in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Agnes was there at the same time, was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I must remind you again, sir, that when we speak about Mr. Agnes, we refer to him by that name, all right? That's important. So you met Jasna --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ryneveld, the witness has actually given another name, and I think it will disappear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with this hotel, the witness tells us, Mr. Sahanic, that he was working that night. Was he living in Bosanski Samac and spent the night in the hotel? Because he said he met him at the hotel. Could he tell us how did it come about that he was in the hotel when he was already working in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I was working in Bosanski Samac, but that is where we were staying. We were accommodated in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear, while you were a policeman, you were staying at the hotel in Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were staying as a guest of that hotel, you occasionally ran into the person known as Mr. Agnes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the night when you met Jasna, were you working? Were you on duty that evening?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I think I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your recollection is that Mr. Agnes was present that night when you first met Jasna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that first meeting result in a further relationship with Jasna? Did you get to know her better over time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, one could say we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would share with us what relationship, if any, developed after your first meeting with Jasna.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, from our first meeting, as she was living in Bosanski Samac, we would frequently see each other, and I think the relationship became stronger, closer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How close a relationship -- I don't mean to pry, sir, but how close a relationship did you develop with Jasna, and up to the point of the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become friends?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How close friends did you become?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: We were close, so close that we didn't really see each other every day but almost every day, and we went out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to ask if you had become boyfriend and girlfriend?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could call it that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've mentioned earlier in your testimony that -- when I asked you about when the war started, you indicated that something happened the night of the 16th or 17th. Did something happen to you that particular night or morning of the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: On the first day after the beginning of the war in Bosanski Samac, I was captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "captured," exactly what do you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: It means that on that day, I think it was in the afternoon, I was taken into custody in the street by paramilitary units and taken to the police station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These paramilitary units, could you identify what kind of units these were? Were they wearing uniforms of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, to judge by their speech, they were not from those parts. I think they were not from Bosnia-Herzegovina. To judge by their accent, I would say that they came from Serbia. At that moment, I didn't notice any insignia, except that they were wearing very worn uniforms and they had black woollen caps on their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly were you when you were, as you put it, captured?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: At the moment I was captured, I was right next to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you alone or was someone with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I was with Mr. Agnes at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what time of day it was that you were captured?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, maybe around 2.00 or 3.00, or maybe even 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how you were dressed; i.e., were you in uniform or in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I was in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two of you, Mr. Agnes and yourself, were right beside the hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment, we were right beside the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you had been doing up until the point in time that you were captured? I don't mean you to go back that far, but how was it that you happened to be outside the hotel with Mr. Agnes at the moment you were captured? Where had you been? What had you been doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: We were outside, and Mr. Agnes and I wanted to seek shelter near the banks of the River Sava, to wait for nightfall, and then to get out of there somehow, but something happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you looking for shelter? Shelter from what?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: We were afraid of these people who arrived in Bosanski Samac, captured the police station. We heard shooting from the bridge, so we thought it would be best to lie low and wait for the right moment to get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that afternoon -- that is, the afternoon of the 17th of April -- when had you last seen Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: It was just before that, before the attack on Samac, which means during the night, the night of the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under what circumstances had you been with Jasna, and how did you leave her?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I think that evening we were in a discotheque that was close to the hotel. I don't know exactly what time it was when I saw her home, and that was the last time I saw her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw her home, had there been an outbreak of fighting yet?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No. I returned to the hotel after that and fell asleep. I don't know for how long I slept. I was awakened by banging on my room's door by the receptionist who was working at the hotel there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear in my mind, sir, so I understand what you've said, you were out with Jasna for the evening, you saw her home, you went to the hotel, went to sleep, and were awakened by the receptionist. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what time of day it would have been that you were awakened by the receptionist?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it could have been about 2.00 a.m., something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you awakened by the receptionist?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: She woke me up because she knew I was working in the police station there, and probably for security reasons she woke me up so that I would be awake. I think she did it for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, was it clear that the war had started?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I think it was clear by then, because that is how it started in most other cities. There were many towns in which the war started in the same way, so that it was clear to the people in this town, too, that the war had begun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you weren't originally from Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that you were stationed at Bosanski Samac as part of your police duties?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked in Bosanski Samac within the frameworks of a sort of subcommand. That is to say, it was before the beginning of the war in Bosanski Samac. There were problems there with regard to the crossing of a bridge there across the Sava River, and I was sent there. It was a sort of special unit to provide security for the bridge so as to avoid any conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was one of your duties as a policeman when you were sent to Bosanski Samac; that is, to guard the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the main tasks was that one, although we had other duties as well, the kind of work that people in my profession do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Sahanic, after the receptionist awakened you, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Immediately after she woke me up, I heard strong shooting from the direction of the bridge and, later on, from the direction of the police station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What actions, if any, did you take?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I went downstairs to the reception desk, and there were many other guests there who had been spending the night in the hotel. I suggested that it would be best for us to take shelter in a room that was not turned towards the police station and bridge, because I thought that there might be some sort of bombing or shelling and that we would be safer, the people there would be safer, those people who had been in the hotel during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among these people did you see Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agnes was present as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without going into a great deal of detail about what you did in the hours after being awakened, I take it, though, that you and Mr. Agnes spent some time together after you assembled -- after being awakened by the receptionist.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between that time and the time that you were captured together outside the hotel, did you ever see Jasna again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to skip over some of the details of what happened, sir, but you told us that you were captured; and by "captured", do you mean actually physically arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, if by "physically arrested" you mean when someone comes in front of you with a rifle and orders you to put your hands up and run to the police station, then it could be said to be physically arrested or as you yourself termed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that was the way in which you were told to go to the police station, the way you've just described, at rifle point?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Agnes with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was. We were together. Both of us had to put our hands up and go to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go through this in detail, sir, but I'm going to ask, where were you taken? Perhaps you could trace it for us very quickly. You went from being captured to a location and, I understand, to a number of other locations over a period of time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, in a summary form, tell us where you went and where you eventually ended up?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, while I was made to run towards the police station, they put me into one of the cells that were there for provisional detention, and I spent that night there, and I think already the next day that I was transferred to another premises across the road from the police station. This was a smaller building that was called the Territorial Defence building. I think that I spent some seven to ten days there. I'm not quite certain exactly how long. But afterwards I was transferred to Brcko by them, to the barracks there, the army barracks at Brcko. I spent only a few days there. After that, I was once again transferred to Bijeljina, from Bijeljina once again, after some five or six days -- I'm not quite sure how long -- they took us to Ugljevik, and at Ugljevik I spent some five or six days. I was returned to Bijeljina. Several days later, back to Bosanski Samac, where I stayed until the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During all of the time that you were transferred from place to place, as you outlined for us, do you know where Mr. Agnes was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agnes spent the whole time, except the several days that I spent in Ugljevik. He was in the group with me, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you indicated you went from place to place to place and ended up back at Bosanski Samac, Mr. Agnes was with you for most of that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to Bosanski Samac, where were you detained?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: As soon as I returned, we were detained for one night in a hall next to the large gym/sports hall of the elementary school, and then we were transferred to the gym of the elementary school. That's what it was called, the gym hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The elementary school or the primary school, is that the building you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I mean the sports and gym hall attached to the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, sir, you have outlined to us that you were captured on the 17th of April, and you've outlined again for us where you went for a number of days. Is it safe to assume, from what you've told us, that it's now May of 1992 when you ended up at the elementary or primary school?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I think it was May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the elementary school, this gymnasium, was Mr. Agnes detained with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agnes was also detained with me on the premises of the gymnasium of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained with him, while you were jointly prisoners there, did your relationship with Mr. Agnes continue? I mean did you become friends over that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately before the war broke out in Bosanski Samac, we were friends, and I think that everything we experienced in our joint detention made us even stronger friends perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not at this time intend to ask you any details about your detention. I'm not going to get into that. But while you were detained with Mr. Agnes at the elementary school after May of 1992, did you have occasion to see the person I've referred to as Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, I did. She came there; I think she brought some sandwiches or something to eat. So I saw her once while I was in the gym hall of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She brought you some sandwiches, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I think it was a sandwich or something else. Anyway, something to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said I wouldn't get into any of the details, but I have to ask something in order to put this into perspective. Was it customary for people to bring you food from outside the detention camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not permitted, but if somebody before the war, of the people living in Samac, had a good relationship with the guards, then they were able to bring in some food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, generally speaking, what the ethnic background of the guards was? Do you know whether they were Bosnians or Croats or Serbs? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Apart from one Serb, all the rest were Muslims or Croats; in detention, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the guards.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that from your answer. I'm sorry that I didn't make myself clear. Do you know the ethnic background of the guards? If you don't know, just say you don't know, but I wondered whether you knew.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, I think most of them were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what Jasna's ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I think she was a Catholic, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Agnes around when Jasna brought you the sandwich?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he was around when she brought the sandwich, but he was on the same premises where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he have been in a position to see or to know if she had brought you the sandwich?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether he was in a position to see, but later on, he was in a position to know. I told him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Ryneveld, that the witness could surely go a little quicker through your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because some of the things, surely, can be done more expeditiously to economise with the time of the Trial Chamber, because I think to go into such detail is not so helpful. So I think that the examination should be conducted in a way as to go directly to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour. I will certainly expedite matters. I thought some of these matters were of significance, but I have Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think in that regard, Mr. Ryneveld, you should consider whether you could lead in relation to matters that are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I contemplated that, Your Honour, but not having had an opportunity to determine which of these issues is contentious and which are not, I thought it would be best if I took the cautious route and not exceed the bounds of leading evidence. I know it's leading in chief, but I didn't know I could lead in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But surely it's a question of whether they are relevant, not whether they are contentious. It's very difficult to see what this has to do with what we are investigating here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have Your Honour's point. I will move on and I will take heed to your instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sahanic, I understand, sir, that there was a second occasion as well when you saw Jasna, is that correct, while you were still detained with Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that in fact Jasna had arranged for you and Mr. Agnes to leave the detention centre and work for one of the guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that second incident, did you see Jasna again, or was that the last time you saw her?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: That was the last time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I also understand that you continued in detention with Mr. Agnes until the 5th of November of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Until the 5th of November, 1992, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, sir, you were exchanged, as they call it, and you got to leave the institution or the detention camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left, to your knowledge, Mr. Agnes remained behind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since leaving Mr. Agnes behind on the 5th of November of 1992, have you seen him again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after you were exchanged, I understand that you went to Tuzla, where you dated other women and you met and married your present wife; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: For a short space of time, I stayed near Orasje, and then I went to Tuzla, yes, and I did see other women, dated them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You ultimately met and married your wife, is that correct, your present wife?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work as a policeman after being exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: After the exchange, until I went to Germany, I worked as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to Germany in August of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you did not hear from Mr. Agnes until -- well, for the next six years after you last saw him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the autumn of 1998 -- I'm taking you to Germany and it's now the autumn of 1998 -- did you continue to have regular telephone conversations with your mother, who lived in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On one of those occasions, sir, I understand that you went to a pay phone and telephoned your mother; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, in addition to your usual discussions with your mother, she told you something that was new and interesting to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I choose not to lead in this area, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your mother told you that is of interest to the Court today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, she told me that a few days before I called her up, in her house where she lives in Tuzla, that a young man and a young girl came and that the man introduced himself, although she forgot the name he said, but he said he knew me. He said he had been detained with me together in Bosanski Samac. My mother invited them in for a cup of coffee, as is customary. They went in, had a cup of coffee. The young man and the young woman were interested in knowing where I was. My mother said I was in Germany, she showed them my pictures from the photo album, and the young man asked for one of those photographs, my photograph, which my mother gave him. She even gave them my telephone number and address in Germany because he said he'd like to hear me. They left. The girl went towards the car that was parked there, the car in which they had come, and the young man stayed behind. He was busy putting on his shoes, and when he went away, he told my mother, "Well, let me tell you something. I want to disclose a secret. The girl with me used to be Mirsad's girlfriend in Bosanski Samac," and that was what that meeting was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your mother told you this on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time your mother told you this, had you ever heard from Jasna since you last saw her when you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No, I had no news from her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after speaking to your mother sometime -- oh, do you know exactly when it was you spoke to your mother?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but it could have been in mid 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sometime after speaking to your mother about that incident that you've just told us about, did you get a call in the early morning hours from Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: You mean after the girl had been to see my mother?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agnes phoned me after my conversation with my mother. It was sometime at the end of 1998 or the beginning of 1999, perhaps even February 1999. I'm not quite sure as regards the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not sure as to when these phone calls happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say for sure, couldn't give you the exact month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit about the first telephone call from Mr. Agnes? What was said by whom?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: That night, Mr. Agnes phoned me up, late at night -- it was sometime around 2.00 a.m. or 1.00 a.m. -- and during the conversation, Mr. Agnes throughout -- that is to say, I thought that Mr. Agnes blamed me for the fact that he stayed on in detention, and he thought that after I had been exchanged, I could have possibly taken him out, got him out, and he said his life was finished, that he was in a wheelchair, that he wasn't able to move around. That whole conversation boiled down to his accusations of me for not having pulled him out of prison, and he thought that after I had been exchanged, that I could have done that perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first time you heard from Mr. Agnes after you had seen him last on the 5th of November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction to getting a phone call from him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was happy to hear from him after so many years, but afterwards, it was rather unpleasant. I was sorry that he was blaming me for not pulling him out of prison. And he didn't realise what the situation was like, because it was absolutely impossible to pull anybody out of gaol, even if you did have connections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That call was in the early morning hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were awakened from a sleep by that call?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was sleeping when the phone rang.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the phone conversation last, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: It lasted a long time, perhaps some 40 minutes even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from Mr. Agnes again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear from him again, once more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how much later after that first early morning phone call?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. Perhaps one or two months after the first call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what transpired during that second telephone call from Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: During the second phone call, the conversation changed a little bit. Mr. Agnes did not put so much blame on me for not getting him out any longer, and we spoke about regular things. He asked me how I was doing and, as I was married, he asked about my children. So it touched more on regular things. It was not a conversation in which he was accusing me of not getting him out of prison, as was the case in the first conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your telephone conversation with Mr. Agnes, was he the only person you spoke to in that phone call?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: During the second phone call, I first talked to Mr. Agnes, and then he asked me, "Do you know who is next to me?" I could assume, I thought it was Jasna, and so I said so, and then I continued to talk to Jasna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a reason why you assumed that Jasna was next to him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I thought that it was him who had visited my mother with Jasna, and so I assumed that she may have been there with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently find out whether or not that was true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Later on, I learned that it was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Jasna told me so during one of our conversations. She said it was Mr. Agnes and she said it was one of her friends, and she mentioned a name but I did not remember the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, in your conversation with Mr. Agnes, you, in response to this question, "Do you know who's next to me?" you guessed it was Jasna and you turned out to be correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: The remainder of the conversation I spent talking to Jasna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the conversation about?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: We spoke for the first time then about some regular things. I asked her what was new with her, and she asked me what was new with me, how I lived and so on. During this second conversation when Mr. Agnes called, my conversation with Jasna was very brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of that conversation, was it clear to you why she wanted to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought, the first time I talked to her, that is, that after everything that we had before the war, that she wanted to talk to me. And she said it would be nice if I came to Bosnia so we could see each other, and I thought at first that it was her wish to see me again and to talk with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she make it clear to you that she wanted to see you again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Not that clear, but in the course of the subsequent conversations, the gist of all these conversations was that she wanted me to come back to Bosnia and to see me again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to subsequent conversations, so we'll go to those in just a moment. How long did this conversation that was started by Mr. Agnes, and the phone handed off to Jasna, how long did that telephone conversation last?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It could have been about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where she was phoning from or where Mr. Agnes was phoning from?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: That I wouldn't know exactly, where they called from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you hear from Jasna again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: After that conversation, I had perhaps another four calls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. From whom?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. You said that she called you again on subsequent occasions; is that correct? When was the next call; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: The next conversation may have been two or three weeks later, after the call when I talked both to Mr. Agnes and to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the conversation about?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked about this and that. She kept repeating, "When are you going to come, when am I going to see you," and she said, "Well, you got married and made promises to each other." But for the most part, she wanted me to say firmly when I would come back to Bosnia. I said that given the memories of my last days in Samac, I wasn't sure that I wanted to go back there any time soon, and she said that I shouldn't worry about it, that she was in charge there. I don't know what she meant about that, but she gave me firm guarantees that I would be perfectly safe if I came back there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ryneveld, could we learn from the witness where these phone calls were made, where he received those phone calls?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you got the phone calls?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I received those telephone calls on my mobile telephone which I had at the time. Sometimes I was in different locations. I may not have been home all the time. I may have been in town. But they all came -- they were all made to my mobile phone when I was not at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give her your mobile number?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: During the conversation with Mr. Agnes and Jasna, it was then that I gave them my mobile phone number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me see if I understand, sir. You're married and you have two children?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife then know about Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: She knew of my previous relationship with her, but she did not know of the subsequent calls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you want Jasna phoning you at your home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that why you gave your mobile number?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how often would she phone you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but she may have called up to twice a week. Then perhaps there would be a pause of seven to ten days, and then there were again a couple of calls a week and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so on. And this went between what period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: It may have lasted for over a month, perhaps less than two months. I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the general theme of the phone calls? What was it that Jasna wanted you to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: From what I could gather, she wanted -- she became resigned to the fact that our relationship could not go on because I was married and that perhaps we should become more like friends, and she wanted to see me. She always asked me to come, and to give her some firm promise as to when I could come, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When she called you, how long were these phone calls, generally speaking? Were they short, long, intermediate?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: You could describe them as very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the cost of telephone calls from Bosanski Samac to Germany?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how much it costs from Bosanski Samac, but a minute of conversation from Tuzla, which is very close to Samac, costs somewhere between two and three German marks per minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever comment to Jasna about the price of the phone calls that she was spending on you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: On one occasion during these first few conversations, when I saw that the conversation was going on and on, I asked her who was going to pay for this, that maybe we should hang up and she could call again a few days later. She said that it wasn't material, how long it took, when it concerned me. And then I don't know whether she had money to pay this, but obviously she was not particularly concerned, how much she was going to pay for it and how long the conversations were going to last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your conversations with Jasna, did she tell you what she did for a living now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: She didn't tell me what she was doing exactly. I did ask her, though, what she did, and she was a bit secretive. She said that she was working, that she travelled a lot, but she wouldn't tell me specifically what exactly the nature of her job was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that when she was trying to persuade you to come to Bosanski Samac, she had indicated something about her being an important person? Those are my words now, but perhaps you could tell us what she said about that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: In that regard, during the conversation when I said that I feared coming back to Samac to see her again, she said that she was in charge there, that nobody would touch me, that she had some people who were important, who were in high positions, and I don't know what she meant by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to back up to something that I neglected to ask you a moment ago, and we'll come back to this, but did you hear from Mr. Agnes again during the course of these various telephone conversations with Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss Mr. Agnes with Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, the discussions that you had with Jasna about Mr. Agnes? Perhaps I should -- first of all, did you have any discussions with her about her getting any identification from Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what you meant by "identification."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you could explain to us this way: During the course of her explaining to you that she was an important person in Bosanski Samac, was there any discussions about requests Mr. Agnes may have made of her that she would assist in arranging?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: When we spoke about Mr. Agnes, I asked her what he did. She said that he would come for a few days and then disappear again. And he mentioned a case when he requested that she provide him with some documents -- I think it was a personal identity card in the police station -- and she said that he was a bit upset that she couldn't provide it to him so fast, even though she commented that he received it much faster than was the regular procedure. Then we also talked about some additional things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to back up again for a moment. In these telephone conversations with Jasna, you told us earlier that she told you, in a later call, that she, in fact, had gone to visit your mother with a friend and that it was not Mr. Agnes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she ever tell you how it was that she knew where your mother lived?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: She said that she was wandering about Tuzla for two days, going from one police station to the next, and even went to the police headquarters in Tuzla, and she asked to be received by the chief of police. I don't know if she succeeded in that, but she received information, because previously I had worked at that police station, and thus she was able to first receive the information regarding the address and then the phone number subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So she went to various police stations to track you down; is that correct? That's what she told you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes. In her own words, she said that she had got the whole police force going in order to locate me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, since you worked for the police, you had some records there about where your mother lived. Is that how the information became available?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Of course, there is information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your discussions with Jasna, where she wanted you to meet with her in Bosanski Samac, did you ever agree to go to Bosanski Samac, in particular?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I never told her a precise time because I myself did not know. The situation is difficult for the refugees to travel from Germany; some are lucky enough to get a visa to travel, but some never do. I said that perhaps I would come in August, but I never considered that I really had to go there so fast and meet her. I had contemplated going to Bosnia that fall with the family, and I never told her exactly when. I said August, September, and then she said, "Well, you said August," and then another time, I would say, "Maybe September, October."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just so that I'm clear, when were you having these telephone conversations with Jasna? Was it in 1998 or 1999 that you were talking to Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: This was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you're talking about coming in the fall of 1999, that would have been just last August, is that what you're saying; last September, last August, two, three months ago?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I may have misspoken about mentioning 1998. What I had in mind was to come back to Bosnia in 1999, around this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. These conversations with Jasna happened until when? When was the last time you spoke with Jasna on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It could have been May 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May 1999. All right. Had you discussed a tentative meeting at some village near Bosanski Samac at any point?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: When I said that I feared coming back to Bosanski Samac, she said that it didn't matter, that if I didn't want to come there, that we could have met any other place within the federation, Tuzla or some other place, but the important thing was for me to come back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm going to back you up a little bit. A couple of months after your second telephone call from Mr. Agnes, okay, not the first call in the middle night but the second call from Mr. Agnes, sometime after that, after you had first spoken to Jasna, did you get another call in the middle of the night from an unknown person, not Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, and it was also late. I don't know what time, but let's say around midnight, I received a call from a person. The conversation lasted a very short time. When I picked up the phone, he said, "Why aren't you calling Bosnia? You know who is there." And while I sort of came to and sort of asked, "Who is this?" he said, "Go back to sleep" and also some swear words. So it was a very brief conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say there were some swear words. First of all, let me break this up a little bit. Did you know who the person was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No. No, I could not recognise the voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it male or female?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: It was a male voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was not Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm 90 per cent certain it was not his voice. My first impression when I heard the voice was that it was not his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person, whoever it was, woke you up in the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Called you an insulting name.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then said something about, "Why aren't you calling Samac," words to that effect, is that correct, "Do you know who you have there?"

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he said specifically, whether he said, "Why don't you call Bosanski Samac?" I don't recall whether he said "Samac" or "Bosnia," because I was not fully awake. Then he said a few additional insulting words, and then he said, "Go back to sleep."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand why you were being called, sir, as a result of that telephone call? Did you understand why you were being phoned?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: At first, I thought that Jasna perhaps expected me to call her sometime and that she perhaps was sitting somewhere, in some cafe with some friends, and that she may have asked them to call me. So at first, I thought that it was all her doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever call Jasna?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: You mean after that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ever.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was always her phoning you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In mid May, did you get another call from Jasna, mid May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: There were several additional conversations, the last one of which was, I believe, in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very last telephone call you got from Jasna, whenever that was in May, can you tell us what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked about all kinds of things, but again, it all boiled down to my coming there, that I would be safe there. The last time, I asked her what she did, and believe that during that very last conversation, she mentioned she was looking for a piece of clothing. There was nothing in Samac that she liked, so she was talking about going to Tuzla because there were more boutiques there where she could find that kind of stuff. Again, the conversation centred on her trying to have me commit to a particular time when I would come there. Then she also said that an occasion could be created for us to see each other somewhere else and that this could be perhaps -- and she mentioned the end of August, early September, that she was waiting for someone to tell her about some, I believe she called it, business trip to the Netherlands and that she could arrange for this man to maybe help her cross the border and that I could come to the Dutch border myself and that we could meet there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we're going to take the break at 4.00, so when you come to a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm nearly finished, but I wouldn't mind consulting with my colleagues. Perhaps this would be a convenient time for the break, and I should only be, I would say, no more than five minutes, unless you wish me to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I understand that you'd prefer to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, not really, Your Honour. If you wanted the break now, I could. This would be a convenient time. I'm quite happy to ask about five more questions and be done, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will go ahead. Judge Hunt wants to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, this may be something you can deal with after the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- but I'm curious to know where all this evidence fits in. I understand, having looked at the statements, that you seem to be suggesting that Mr. Avramovic lined all this up through Jasna and that Mr. Agnes was involved. Whereabouts is it in, if I may so call them, the charges? You see, these documents were filed after the scheduling order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The charges are in fairly specific terms. They are based upon the statements that have been filed up to that time, or at least those parts of them that was thought should be included, but none of this is in any of the charges. Is it put forward as some sort of similar fact evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It's certainly being put forward as a body of evidence from which this Court may have to decide the issue of credibility of the main witness. The main witness has put forward allegations. Those allegations, of course, depend on credibility. Insofar as parts of his testimony are capable of corroboration, it is incumbent on us to lead evidence of those elements that are capable of corroboration, and it is for this Chamber to find whether or not you are satisfied about the witness's credibility or reliability about those areas where there is some possibility of corroborating his evidence. Needless to say, many of these other matters are done in such a situation that it would be a "he said/he said" kind of situation. So this evidence is clearly relevant to the issue of the credibility of the main witness, and I will, of course, be happy to try to expand on that, but insofar as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, you've made it clear. You're not seeking in any way to expand the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Not whatever, no. The charges are rise and fall on the basis of Mr. Agnes's testimony, but it's clearly relevant for this Court to make the ultimate determination as to what, if any, of Mr. Agnes's evidence you will believe by virtue of looking at the other issues where there is some capability of corroboration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not clear now whether you wanted me to proceed or whether we should have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, talking, if we may, just about that last comment about her travelling, did I understand you correctly to say that she indicated to you that she was coming to the Netherlands in August or September of 1999? That was the plan?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, she said that she would travel to the Netherlands with a man, she didn't know exactly when, but she believed it was late August, early September, and that we could arrange somehow -- that she could arrange with the man for her to be taken to the Dutch/German border and that I could come to the German border too and that we could meet there somehow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is in May of 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this conversation took place -- that this took place during my last conversation with her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard from Jasna again, since mid May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During one of your conversations with Jasna about her travelling, did she ever indicate to you what she was doing for her livelihood, what her business was, what she was doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Through the conversation, I learned that she had a coffee bar in Bosanski Samac and that she intended to buy another one, that she also travelled a lot with people, but she did not specifically tell me what she did actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She said she owned this cafe herself, this cafe or coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, she said so, and her boyfriend -- I don't know whether they owned it together or whether they just worked together there, but that she was at least a part owner of that coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So she told you she had a boyfriend.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she ever give you the telephone number of the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the various telephone calls that you had from her, could you ever tell whether she was calling from the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Whenever she called, most of the calls that she made, I believe, were not from the cafe, based on what you could hear as background noises, because this conversation took a long time. There were one or two conversations that were made from the cafe because you could hear background noise, and also she put down the receiver to go and get some drinks. But several times, I could gather that she wasn't calling from the cafe because there was silence in the background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you spoke to Mr. Agnes and he handed the phone off to Jasna, could you tell whether that was one of those silent backgrounds or whether it was a noisy cafe background?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure with respect to that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, if I may, just to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Ryneveld. Before consulting your colleagues, I should like you to ask the witness whether he himself, throughout this period, did he ever call Jasna directly? Did he take the initiative and call her?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe I did ask that question, but I'll ask it -- maybe I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever telephone Jasna yourself, Mr. Sahanic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: I never personally called Jasna to talk to her. Even though when she called, several times, I was working in Berlin at the time, and if she called when I was at work, I asked her to call later; and if I was finished with work, I just called her and let the phone ring once or twice, and that was a signal for her to call me, but I never made a call to her to talk to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So each time you spoke to her, she was the one who originated the call.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD SAHANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sahanic. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take the adjournment now and resume at half past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll continue. I ask whether there is any cross-examination from any of the concerned parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: None on behalf of Todorovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: None on behalf of Mr. Tadic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None on behalf of Mr. Zaric either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no cross-examination either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the circumstances, we'll take the adjournment until tomorrow afternoon. At the commencement of those proceedings, we will have the head of the Victims and Witnesses Unit come to provide whatever information he can in relation to the matter at hand. So we adjourn now until tomorrow afternoon at 2.30. Ms. Paterson, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to bring to your attention, we do have another witness ready to testify today, if you would like to proceed with him. He's a short witness, and we believe we could conclude him quite easily within an hour or less. So we would be happy to proceed with him, if you would like, or if you prefer, we could bring him back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is that witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: The investigator, Tore Soldal, from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, call Mr. Soldal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Then we're finished with Mr. Sahanic, and the Office of the Prosecutor would call Investigator Tore Soldal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Before we break, would the Court entertain a speaking motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In relation to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: With regard to the Court's decision of July 27th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What decision is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: That was the decision on the Prosecution's ex parte application which was unsealed by Your Honour's order of October 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, that is not a matter that is related to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: None at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not disposed to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness will make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Paterson. Examined by Ms. Paterson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Soldal. Will you please state your full name and spell your name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Tore Soldal. T-O-R-E, S-O-L-D-A-L.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I just say this witness can be led, so far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sure you'll take account of that, Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate the Court's desire to expedite the proceeding, and I can assure you we will get through Mr. Soldal's testimony as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Court, Mr. Soldal, where you currently work and what position you hold?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I'm an investigator at the OTP, team 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention, Mr. Soldal, to the 6th of May, this year, 1999. On that date, did you have an occasion to meet a man who has been referred to for this proceeding as Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I would like to ask the clerk to show you this piece of paper. If you would just look at the name on this paper, Mr. Soldal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think this has been established by now, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's just get on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we can move on. It's not an issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I appreciate moving on, Your Honours, but we're also appreciative of trying to make a record. Should there ever be an appeal in this proceeding, we would like the record to be full and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There has been no dispute at any time about any of this, Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, is the person who's named on that piece of paper the man that you know as Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe for the Court, briefly, the circumstances under which you came to meet Mr. Agnes on the 6th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It was on mission in Tuzla. I got a phone call from our Sarajevo office, and they told me that an American army camp outside Brcko had called them and said that they had a person who had information about possible war crimes in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then proceed to the SFOR base and meet Mr. Agnes at that location?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: This was in the afternoon, and I called my team leader in The Hague. She told me to go to the army camp the day after, so I brought my interpreter and went to the camp the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Agnes at the camp, how did he introduce himself to you? Did he show you any identification?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No, he didn't show me any identification when he was introduced to me because all his papers were taken care of by the camp officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time, did you see an identification from Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the intelligence officer in the camp to show me all the documents he brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those documents all in the name that was on that piece of paper that you looked at before?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Agnes at the SFOR base and in subsequent conversations, did he inform you that he was also known by another name?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: He told me that in Serbia, he used a Serbian name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court what that name was?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Damir Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he explain to you why he used this different name?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: He told me that it was after a suggestion from his uncle, and he had told him that he could live an easier life in Serbia with a Serb name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever show you any identification in the name of Damir Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: He told me that he had identification but he didn't brought [sic] it to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please describe to the Court the demeanour -- the behaviour of Mr. Agnes when you first met him at the SFOR camp in May?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: He was very nervous, and when I asked him to give us an interview, he told me that he was afraid for his life and for his relatives in Serbia. So he wanted actually protection in the army camp before he was willing to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your impression that Mr. Agnes was, in fact, afraid at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: For me, he seemed very afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time after you met him, did you take a formal written statement from Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: In the beginning, he wasn't willing to give us a statement because he wanted to know whether he could stay in the camp or not, and I discussed that with him. The agreement was that I could interview him, I could type it, but he wasn't willing to sign it before he knew whether he could stay in the camp or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask anything else of you in return for giving you a statement?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No, he never asked for anything else than this protection from the army camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever ask you for money?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever ask you to be relocated to another country?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you to be provided with a job?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only thing he asked you for was security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then, in fact, take a written statement from Mr. Agnes that he agreed to sign?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes. This happened during several days. We started in the army camps for two days. Then my team leader in The Hague told me to take him to Sarajevo, and I stayed together with him in an apartment there until it was decided what to do. He actually signed the statement before he knew anything about the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the statement that you took from him, did he tell you about an incident in which he acquainted him and accidentally discharged his gun, and a young woman had been shot as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that when I interviewed him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that as a result of that shooting incident, he was subsequently placed in gaol in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that at some point in time, his uncle assisted him to get out of gaol by making some money payments to some people?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you took that first statement from Mr. Agnes, did you take other statements from him as well?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Altogether, I took five statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did he explain to you at some point in time that the first statement he gave you, he may not have been completely forthcoming in the information that he had to provide, that he perhaps had left some things out of that first statement?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: The first statement, after he signed it, I went back to The Hague two days after he signed it, and he come one week after me to The Hague. And then we had a meeting, and he told me that he had some more information but he couldn't tell it because he was afraid of the safety for his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took a second statement from him, what was the substance of that statement about?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
